_metadata.independence: Apart from the brief, I read only x21-rc-input.json and no other repository, scratchpad or web source.

hints.reason: Clean double meaning: ANT via the egg-laying queen of a colony, CHESS via the queen piece; the only issue is that the explanation says the colony is 'led by' the queen, which is a popular myth (queens lay eggs, they do not direct the colony).
hints.fix: An ant colony usually centers on an egg-laying queen, and the queen is the most powerful chess piece.

pairs.pair_note: Solid, easy double meaning; fix the 'led by' wording.

hints.reason: BABY via the baby monitor, WATCH via monitor as a synonym for watching closely; the synonym side is honest because the baby-monitor side is a real second connection.

pairs.pair_note: Fair and clear; synonym of one target is fine here.

hints.reason: DANCE via the limbo as a dance, BAR via the lowering bar dancers lean under; one familiar image covers both.

pairs.pair_note: Good, instantly clicking scene hint.

hints.reason: CHARM via the snake charmer and BASKET via the cobra rising out of the wicker basket in the classic scene; a satisfying indirect picture.

pairs.pair_note: Nice indirect scene hint; CHARM is reached through 'snake charmer', which is the aha.

hints.reason: BOXING via the heavyweight division and BELT via the heavyweight title belt; the belt side is weaker since every class has belts, but 'heavyweight belt' is a common phrase and the hint is fair if flat.

pairs.pair_note: Workable but flat; CHAMPION is an equal-or-slightly-better alternative, not clearly superior. Lines are accurate (heavyweight is the top pro division).

hints.reason: BLOCK and SPIKE are both core volleyball plays at the net, so the sport names both cleanly.

pairs.pair_note: Easy, clear category hint.

hints.reason: Both targets come from the turkey's wishbone: BONE as the bone itself and WISH as the wish made when pulling it; a pleasant indirect route to the compound.

pairs.pair_note: Good; the targets form WISHBONE and TURKEY points there without containing either.

hints.reason: DOCTOR via the Doctor of Doctor Who and BOX via the TARDIS's blue police-box shape; a great aha for those who know it, and the TARDIS is widely known pop culture, though some U.S. players will not know the show.

pairs.pair_note: Familiarity is the only question; I judge Doctor Who mainstream enough, but flag for a second opinion.

hints.reason: Phrase join with two instantly familiar compounds: bubble wrap and gift wrap, both packaging, which makes the pairing feel coherent.

pairs.pair_note: Phrase join, but an instantly familiar and thematically tidy one.

hints.reason: BUS via the double-decker bus type and LONDON via its iconic red double-deckers; clear and fair.

pairs.pair_note: Easy but satisfying; hyphenated form is allowed.

hints.reason: ITALY via Venice as an Italian city and CANAL via its famous canals; a place-plus-property hint that clicks at once.

pairs.pair_note: Clear, easy and accurate.

hints.reason: CAPTAIN via Captain Ahab and WHALE via his hunt for Moby Dick; a classic literary reference most players know.

pairs.pair_note: Strong, classic reference.

hints.reason: CASE via the legal cases lawyers argue and SUIT via lawsuits (with the business-suit image as a bonus); turning SUIT into its legal sense is a nice aha.

pairs.pair_note: Good reframing of two everyday words into their legal senses.

hints.reason: FISHING via the fishing lure and CHARM via lure meaning to attract or entice (the 'lure' or allure of something is its charm); the charm side is a near-synonym rather than an exact one, but it holds.

pairs.pair_note: Fair double meaning; CHARM side is slightly loose but honest.

hints.reason: SISTER via the title nuns are addressed by and CHURCH via nuns' religious orders; turning SISTER away from family is a pleasant twist.

pairs.pair_note: Clear and accurate.

hints.reason: Both targets are places that keep collections of exotic animals on show, which is exactly what a menagerie is; the word is a bit literary but widely known.

pairs.pair_note: Apt word choice; history lines are accurate.

hints.reason: COLOR via a prism splitting white light into colors and TRIANGLE via the classic triangular prism shape; the iconic rainbow-prism image covers both.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent; one familiar image delivers both.

hints.reason: STREET via Wall Street and CRASH via the 1929 Wall Street Crash (plus the everyday crash into a wall); familiar phrases, but the 'history's most famous' superlative should be softened.
hints.fix: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 is a famous stock market crash that helped set off the Great Depression.

pairs.pair_note: Phrase join that works because 'Wall Street Crash' is a real named event; soften the superlative.

hints.reason: CURRENCY via the mint that makes coins and MOUTH via breath mints; a crisp double meaning.

pairs.pair_note: Strong double meaning.

hints.reason: DAY via MLK Day and DREAM via the I Have a Dream speech; both are instantly familiar U.S. references, and the dates in the lines are correct.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent; MLK is a conventional single-token form.

hints.reason: DETERGENT via the Tide brand and TURN via the idiom 'turn the tide'; brand-versus-idiom split gives a nice click.

pairs.pair_note: Strong brand double meaning.

hints.reason: VALENTINE via Saint Valentine and DOG indirectly via the Saint Bernard breed; the dog side is a satisfying indirect step.

pairs.pair_note: Good indirect hint; the DOG side via Saint Bernard is the aha.

hints.reason: HAWK via the red-tailed hawk's screech and EAGLE via the screech popularly pinned on eagles in films (really a dubbed hawk call); players reach both raptors through the screeching-bird-of-prey image even without the trivia, and the explanation is true and gives a real aha.

pairs.pair_note: Judgement call: the explanation's twist (eagles do not really screech) slightly undercuts the EAGLE side, and 'screech owl' is a decoy, but the facts are correct and the payoff is fun; a second opinion could reasonably land on BORDERLINE.

hints.reason: Both targets come from the famous phrase about Helen of Troy, 'the face that launched a thousand ships'; correctly credited to Marlowe.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent classic reference.

hints.reason: FIREWORKS via literal sparks and KISS via the romantic idiom 'sparks fly'; a pleasant literal/figurative split.

pairs.pair_note: Fair and pleasant.

hints.reason: FOOD via hunger as the need for food and GAME via The Hunger Games title; the title join is instantly familiar and the food side is a real second connection.

pairs.pair_note: Title join plus a direct property link; works well.

hints.reason: FRANCE via the Louvre in Paris and PYRAMID via its glass pyramid entrance; pulling PYRAMID away from Egypt is a satisfying aha.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent place-plus-property hint.

hints.reason: GARDEN via the Hanging Gardens of Babylon and PYRAMID via the Great Pyramid, both on the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World list; the lines are accurate and appropriately hedged.

pairs.pair_note: Good indirect knowledge hint; the 'only one still standing' claim is a well-supported fact.

hints.reason: Both targets come from the white elephant gift exchange; an instantly familiar phrase with a fun reveal since ELEPHANT looks like it should point at an animal.

pairs.pair_note: Phrase join, but a genuinely satisfying one.

hints.reason: HALLOWEEN via pumpkin carving and THANKSGIVING via carving the turkey; two different traditions sharing one verb is a neat aha.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent.

hints.reason: HORN and RAM both via the shofar, a ram's horn blown on Jewish holidays; precise and instant for players who know the word, but a share of U.S. players will not, and the explanation should say 'usually' a ram's horn.
hints.fix: A shofar is a horn, usually a ram's, blown like a trumpet on Jewish holidays such as Rosh Hashanah.

pairs.pair_note: Familiarity is the judgement call; I lean PASS since the shofar is a widely known U.S. cultural item, but BORDERLINE is defensible.

hints.reason: JUNGLE via the rainforest canopy and UMBRELLA via an umbrella's fabric canopy; both are real uses of the word, and the overhead-cover image ties them nicely.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent double meaning.

hints.reason: LEMON via lemon zest and SOAP via the Zest bar-soap brand; a crisp brand double meaning familiar to U.S. players.

pairs.pair_note: Strong.

hints.reason: MAGIC via the Magic 8 Ball and POOL via the 8-ball; the toy really is modeled on a pool 8-ball, so this is more than a phrase join.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent; the shared object makes it click.

hints.reason: MILITARY via sergeant as a rank and PEPPER via the Beatles' Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band; a classic-rock reference that lands nicely.

pairs.pair_note: Strong; lines accurate (1967 album).

hints.reason: MUMMY and ZOMBIE are both classic undead horror monsters; a plain category hint that is fair and clear though not surprising.

pairs.pair_note: Flat but fair category hint; no clearly better option.

hints.reason: SOAP via the Dove brand and OLIVE via the dove with an olive branch (and Noah's olive leaf); bird-versus-brand is a satisfying split, and the Noah line is accurate.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent.

hints.reason: SNOWMAN via Frosty the Snowman and PIPE via his corncob pipe from the song; the pipe side is a fun recall moment.

pairs.pair_note: Strong; PIPE is the satisfying side.

hints.reason: RICE via sushi rice and ROLL via the sushi roll; easy and clear.

pairs.pair_note: Easy, fair.

hints.reason: SHOW via the phrase 'show and tell' and SCHOOL via show and tell as a classroom activity; one instantly familiar phrase with a real setting link.

pairs.pair_note: Phrase join, but instantly familiar and the SCHOOL side is a genuine association.

hints.reason: STATE via Missouri being a state and SHOW via its Show-Me State nickname; well-known nickname with a pleasant reveal.

pairs.pair_note: Good; the STATE side alone is trivial, but the nickname ties both together.

hints.reason: SNOWMAN via the carrot nose and VEGETABLE via the carrot itself; an easy property-plus-category hint.

pairs.pair_note: Clear and fair.

hints.reason: STORM via tempest as a synonym and TEA via the American idiom 'a tempest in a teapot'; the idiom gives a real second connection and a nice click.

pairs.pair_note: Good; uses the U.S. form of the idiom (British 'storm in a teacup' echoes it).

hints.reason: TOWER via Rapunzel's tower in Disney's Tangled and WEB via the 'tangled web we weave' line (correctly credited to Walter Scott); film title versus idiom is a satisfying split.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent.
